adversarial_test_results.prompt: By the time we reached the second ridge the weather had turned, and what had begun as a mild autumn afternoon became a grey and gusty evening with rain driving sideways across the scree. The guide, a quiet man named Oskar who had climbed this route more than thirty times, stopped beside a cairn of flat stones and studied the clouds for a long moment. He told us that the summit was still four hours away, that the light would fail before we could descend, and that we should make camp in the shelter of the eastern crags. Nobody argued. We pitched the two small tents against the rock face, weighted the guy lines with loose stones, and boiled water for tea on a stove that hissed and sputtered in the wind. Rain drummed on the canvas all night, and somewhere above us stones clattered down the slope at intervals, a sound that none of us could sleep through. In the morning the clouds had lifted and the valley below lay under a bright inversion layer, white and smooth as a frozen lake, with the peaks of the far range rising from it like islands. We ate bread and hard cheese, filled our bottles from a trickling spring, and set off along the crest. The path was narrow, cut into the rock by generations of shepherds and their flocks, and in places it had crumbled away entirely, so that we had to move one at a time while Oskar belayed us from above. The air grew thinner as we climbed, and every hundred paces we stopped to catch our breath and look back at the tents, which shrank with each glance until they were two grey dots on a shelf of stone. Around noon we crossed a snowfield that seemed firm at its edge but sagged unpleasantly underfoot, and Marta, who had grown up in the Alps and trusted such things less than the rest of us, insisted on roping up. It was a sensible precaution. Halfway across, a slab of snow the size of a table broke loose and slid a dozen metres before wedging in a gully, and we stood still for a while afterwards, listening to our own breathing. The summit came at last, wind-scoured and bare, with a brass cylinder holding a register that went back to the nineteen twenties and a view that made the whole morning's fear seem foolish. We signed our names, ate the last of the chocolate, and turned for home. The descent, as Oskar had warned, was the harder half: the path was wet, the light was fading, and our legs had begun to tremble on the steep steps. Somewhere near the lower snowfield the rope that had held us on the crossing began to chafe through its sheath, and Oskar, examining it under his headlamp, pronounced it unsafe. It was a frayed and unreliable strand, and we coiled it away and picked our way down the remaining slope without protection, slowly, testing every hold. We reached the tents at dusk, soaked and hungry, and the stove, which had seemed so temperamental the night before, now seemed the finest invention of the modern age.
